chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who hunted game in the open land (al-hill), and it went due to his hunting until it entered the Sanctuary (al-haram), and it died. Is the compensation upon him? He (peace be upon him) said: No, there is no compensation upon him, because he hunted where he hunted, and it was permissible for him. Rather, the example of that is the example of a man who set a snare in the open land next to the Sanctuary, and game fell into it, and the game struggled until it entered the Sanctuary. Thus, there is no compensation upon him, because it was something that happened afterwards. So I said: This is the analogy (qiyas) in the presence of the people. So he (peace be upon him) said: Rather, I compared for you a thing with a thing.

key_terms.الْحَرَمَ: The Sanctuary (specifically Mecca/Medina), where hunting is forbidden
key_terms.الْحِلِّ: The open, permissible land for hunting outside the Sanctuary
key_terms.الْقِيَاسُ: Legal analogy or deductive reasoning used by jurists
key_terms.جَزَاؤُهُ: The compensation or expiation for the hunted game
key_terms.شَرَكاً: A snare or trap set for catching game

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on hunting game in open land that dies inside the Sanctuary?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) establishes that the liability for hunting compensation is determined by the location of the initial act rather than the final resting place of the game, distinguishing this from the strict legal analogy (qiyas) favored by other jurists. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on the specific locus of the obligation, illustrating how physical movement across boundaries does not alter the legal status of the initial action. The comparison to a trap set in the open land further clarifies that the 'cause' of the capture remains within the permissible zone.

en.hubeali: Abu Ali Al Ashary, from Muhammad Bin Al Jabbar, from Safwan Bin Yahya, from Abdul Rahman Bin Al Hajjaj who said,

‘I asked Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> about a man who pelted (stoned) a prey in the unrestricted area. So it went, due to his pelting, until it entered the Al-Harram, and it died. Is there its compensation upon him?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘No, there is no compensation upon him, because he pelted where he pelted, and it was Permissible for him. But rather, the example of that is the example of a man who established a snare in the unrestricted are to the side of the Al-Harram. So a prey falls into it, and the prey wavers until it enters the Al-Harram. Thus, there is no compensation for it upon him, because it was a thing (which happened) afterwards’. 
So I said, ‘This is the analogy in the presence of the people’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘But rather, I<sup>asws</sup> compared for you, a thing with a thing’.
en.sarwar: 12. Abu Ali al-Ash’ariy has narrated from Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who has said the following:

“I once asked abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about a man who shoots a prey in non-al-Haram (the sacred area) and it then moves into al-Haram (the sacred area) and dies there: if he is required to pay ransom. He (the Imam) said, ‘No, he does not owe ransom because he shoots it as he does and it is lawful for him. The example of this is like the one who sets up a trap in an area next to al-Haram (the sacred area). The prey trapped in it moves until it enters al-Haram (the sacred area). He does not owe anything for it; it happened afterwards.’ I then said, ‘This is analogy in the views of people.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘One thing is confused with another thing to you.’”
